facts.text: On this date in 1666, the Great Fire of London broke out — and destroyed 13,200 houses while killing only 6 people, a death toll historians still find implausibly low.
On September 2, 1945, Japan formally surrendered aboard the USS Missouri, ending a war that had killed roughly 3% of the entire world's population.
Mongolia has more horses than people — roughly 4.3 million horses for 3.4 million humans — and many Mongolians still navigate the steppe entirely on horseback.
The Philippines is the only country in Asia where the majority of the population is Christian, a direct legacy of 333 years of Spanish colonial rule.
Tokyo's greater metropolitan area holds 37 million people — more than the entire population of Canada, packed into a region smaller than Connecticut.
On this day in 1929, the Dow Jones peaked at 381 before losing 89% of its value over the next three years. That peak wouldn't be recovered until 1954 — a 25-year wait.
On September 2, 1945, Japan formally surrendered, ending WWII and triggering one of the greatest single-day stock rallies in U.S. history as wartime controls lifted overnight.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792 with just 24 brokers. Its first listed security was Bank of New York stock, which traded at a fixed 0.25% commission.
Saudi Aramco briefly became the first company to hit $2 trillion in market value in 2019 — a figure larger than the entire GDP of Italy, the world's eighth-largest economy.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway once traded below $8 per share. A single Class A share now costs more than $700,000 — making it the most expensive stock on any major exchange.

On this date in 1859, the Carrington Event hit Earth — the most powerful geomagnetic storm ever recorded. Telegraph wires sparked, caught fire, and sent messages without power. The same storm today would collapse global infrastructure within hours.
On September 2, 1969, the first two computers on what became the internet exchanged their first data — at UCLA. The network had two nodes. The first message crashed it.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, but only 1 in 10 of them is human. The rest are bacteria, fungi, and archaea. You are, by cell count, not primarily yourself.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh about a billion tons on Earth — enough to sink through any surface ever conceived.

Light slows down inside glass, water, and other media — but particles can outrun it there. When they do, they emit a blue shock wave called Cherenkov radiation. It is the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.
On this day in 1666, the Great Fire of London began — and burned for four days, destroying 13,200 houses. St. Paul's Cathedral melted. The city it erased was older than the one we rebuilt.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She was separated from the pyramids by more centuries than she is from us.
On this day in 1945, Japan signed the surrender documents aboard USS Missouri, ending WWII. The war in the Pacific outlasted the war in Europe by exactly 99 days.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — 33 years before the telephone. Your grandparents' office ran on technology older than the phone call.
Oxford University began teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. When Montezuma was born, Oxford had already been educating scholars for three centuries.
Meraki (μεράκι): a Greek word for doing something with soul, creativity, and love — leaving a piece of yourself in your work. English has no single equivalent, which says something about English.
Sonder: the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined in 2012 by John Koenig, it spread so fast the dictionary had to chase it.
On this day in 1666, the Great Fire of London was still raging — and the word 'inferno' (from Latin infernus, 'below') originally meant hell itself, not merely a large fire.
Hiraeth (Welsh): a homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or never had. It folds grief, longing, and love into a single syllable cluster English speakers can only approximate.
On September 2, 1945, Japan's formal surrender ended WWII — and the word 'surrender' entered English via Old French se rendre, meaning simply 'to give oneself back.'
On this date in 2017, Bitcoin's price crossed $5,000 for the first time — nine years after Satoshi's whitepaper proposed a system explicitly designed to make trusted third parties obsolete.
On Sep 2, 2015, Ethereum processed its 1,000,000th transaction, just 77 days after mainnet launch — a pace that would have been unthinkable on Bitcoin's UTXO architecture.
The Bitcoin genesis block contains a hidden timestamp: Satoshi embedded a 2009 Times headline about bank bailouts, making the political grievance permanently immutable on-chain.
Ethereum's EIP-1559, live since August 2021, has burned over 4 million ETH — turning the network's fee mechanism into a deflationary force no initial whitepaper anticipated.
The 2016 DAO hack didn't exploit Solidity — it exploited a reentrancy pattern the auditors had flagged. The Ethereum Foundation forked anyway, splitting the chain into ETH and ETC permanently.

On this date in 2009, Hinton's group at Toronto published work on deep belief networks that would directly seed the ImageNet breakthrough three years later — the paper that made 'deep learning' a boardroom word.
On this date in 2017, the first public arxiv draft of 'Attention Is All You Need' was circulating in preprint — the transformer architecture now underlies virtually every frontier language model.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins, roughly every catalogued organism on Earth, in a project that would have taken classical crystallography longer than the age of the universe.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed around 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US households, for a single model training pass.

The first neural network to defeat a human champion at Go, AlphaGo, did so in 2016 using a policy network trained on 30 million expert moves, then refined by playing itself 1.3 million additional games.
